title: Topic clusters without a content mill
metaTitle: Topic clusters without a content mill
excerpt: A cluster is a set of specific answers that link to each other and to one offer. It is not fifty posts with the city name swapped.
alt: Smooth overlapping waves of blue, violet, and warm orange, distinct bands that still belong to one surface.
caption: Overlapping bands of color, separate and still one field. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What is a topic cluster for a studio site?
faqs.answer: It is a small set of specific answers that link to each other and to one offer you actually sell. One page can be the hub. The others go deep on a decision a founder is trying to make. Fifty variations of the same post, with the city or the synonym swapped, are not a cluster.

faqs.question: How many articles belong in a cluster?
faqs.answer: Enough to finish the decisions around one offer, and no more. A handful of strong pages beats a library of thin ones. If you cannot say what the next page decides that the current page does not, do not write it yet.

faqs.question: Where should a cluster point?
faqs.answer: Point the cluster at the offer, the work, or a conversation, in a sentence that matches the page. A reader who needs proof should reach the work, and a reader who is ready to talk should reach a call. The links between the articles should say why the next piece helps, without every article shouting the same call to action.

markdown:
A topic cluster strategy, for a studio, is a set of specific answers that link to each other and to one offer. It is not fifty variations of the same post with the city swapped, and it is not a synonym of your service repeated until a crawler gets tired.

The cluster exists so a founder can finish a decision. If a page does not help that decision, it does not belong in the set.

## Specific answers around one offer

Start from the offer, not from a keyword list. What do you sell, to whom, and what do they have to understand before they hire you? A studio that designs and builds marketing sites might need pages on the brief, the first screen, the redesign, the handoff, and how to read the work. A studio that also designs product interfaces might need a separate set on empty states, errors, and the first screen of a tool. Those are different decisions. They can link. They should not be mashed into one vague article called "digital excellence."

Each page in the cluster should be able to stand alone. Someone will arrive from search on the narrowest one and never see the hub. The first paragraphs have to answer the question. The rest can point sideways, to the sibling that handles the next decision, and onward, to the offer. A page that only makes sense after you read five others is a chapter, not an answer. Publish chapters if you want. Do not expect a stranger to treat them as the front door.

[Google's people-first guidance](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content) is the test to apply before you add another URL. Does this page give original information, a substantial description, and a reason to trust it? Would you share it with a friend? Does the site have a primary purpose, or are you producing lots of content on many topics in the hope that some of it ranks? A cluster passes when every page has a job. It fails when the pages exist to occupy a keyword. The guidance is explicit that writing to a rumored word count, and churning pages to look fresh, is not what the systems are built to reward. Depth is a property of the answer, not of the quota.

Write the offer in a sentence you can repeat. "We design and build the site, and the interface, for a founder who needs the company to be clear." Every essay should be able to point back to that sentence without changing the subject. If an essay cannot, it is a different cluster, or it is a hobby.

## The hub and the spokes

One page can be the map. It names the decision, lists the specific answers, and links to them in sentences. The spokes do the actual teaching. They link back to the map when the reader needs orientation, and they link to one or two neighbors when the next question is obvious. They do not link to everything. A block of twenty "related posts" is how a careful cluster starts to look like a mill.

The hub is not a keyword landing page with thin introductions and no point of view. It should be useful even if the reader never clicks through. A founder should be able to see, from the hub alone, how you think the problem breaks apart. That outline is often the thing they came for. The spokes are for the afternoon they have a specific question.

Choose the hub you already believe. For a studio, the homepage and the services section carry the offer. The cluster should not invent a second offer in order to have a pillar page. If the homepage says you design and build, the cluster should deepen that, not suddenly become a publication about every tool in a modern stack. Name the tools when they change a decision. Next.js, TypeScript, Tailwind, Prisma, PostgreSQL, Vercel: those are true on a Hanabi build, and they belong in an engineering spoke. They do not belong as the title of every spoke.

Keep the URLs stable. A cluster is a set of addresses people and other pages will cite. Renaming a spoke every quarter because a new synonym appeared is how you throw away the links you just earned. If the answer changes, update the page. If the slug was a mistake, redirect it. Do not leave both.

## Why the city swap fails

"Website design in Austin," "website design in Denver," "website design in Portland," written by a studio that works with anyone, is not a cluster. It is one page wearing different hats. The founder in any of those cities can tell. The examples are generic. The constraints are invented. The photos could be anywhere. You have published a template and called it local knowledge.

The same failure happens without cities. "Brand identity for startups," "brand identity for SaaS," "brand identity for fintech," copied forward with the noun replaced, teaches a reader that you will say the same thing to everyone. Sometimes the advice is the same, and the honest move is one page that says so. Split the page when the constraint is real. A heritage editorial site, like Thomas Bewick, is not the same problem as an ecommerce migration, like Down the Cove. A community sports brand, like Ballarat Box Sports, is not the same problem as a product interface like Got Next, Leadly, or Trade Moai. Write those differences. Do not write the category ten times.

[The people-first questions](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content) flag this directly. Are you writing about things because they seem likely to fetch traffic, without real expertise? Are you using automation to produce content on many topics? Would a reader finish and still need to search again? A swapped-city set fails all three. A specific set, drawn from work you have actually done, passes. You do not need a huge portfolio to start. You need to refuse the pages you could generate and did not earn.

## How to choose the set

List the questions a serious buyer asks on the way from stranger to client. Ignore the questions that are only asked by other agencies. You will end up with something like this:

1. What should the first screen of the site do?
2. When is it time to redesign, and what has to stay?
3. What do we need to bring before kickoff?
4. How should we read the portfolio?
5. What do we own when you leave?

That list is already a cluster. Each item can be one strong page. Some items deserve a spoke of their own, such as canonicals, or the sentence under the title in search, because founders now ask those questions before they sign. Add a spoke when a real question does not fit in the parent. Do not add a spoke so the diagram looks impressive in a planning doc.

Stop when the next idea is "we should also rank for" rather than "a founder asked us this, and the answer did not fit." The first is how mills start. The second is how a library starts. Hanabi's writing can sit next to the work: websites, product design, brand, engineering. Those categories are the map. They are not a license to publish a post per permutation.

Write the titles before you write the pages, and read them as a list. If two titles could trade openings, merge them. If a title contains no decision, it is a label, and labels do not deserve a URL. "Thoughts on design" is a label. "What to keep in an ecommerce redesign" is a decision.

## Linking like a person

Inside the cluster, link from a sentence that says why the next page helps. "If the sentence under the title is ready, the next problem is making sure only one URL wears it." That is a link. "Read more" is not. A few of these, chosen, beat a footer full of everything you have ever published.

The link to the offer should match the page. A piece about how to read a portfolio can point at the work. A piece about whether to hire a studio can point at a conversation. A piece about the shape of a marketing site can point at services. The same URL pasted at the bottom of every article, with the same anchor, becomes wallpaper. Readers skip wallpaper. So will you, when you reread the site in six months and notice you have been shouting one sentence in a context where it does not fit.

Do not link every spoke to every other spoke. Pick the path a founder would actually walk. Homepage question, then scope, then proof, then the call. A page about error states in a product does not need to link to a page about RSS, unless you are making a real point about publishing the interface guidelines. Most of the time you are not. Save the link.

Anchor text should sound like the sentence it sits in. "Canonical URLs" is fine if the sentence is about canonical URLs. "Click here for more SEO insights" is how a careful piece starts to sound bought. You are writing to a founder who has read a lot of that voice and left.

## One offer, said plainly

The cluster supports one offer. It does not replace it. At the end of a good path the reader should know what you do and what to do next. They should not feel they have finished a textbook and still do not know whether you take this kind of project. Say it. Design and engineering for the site and the product. A portal afterward for brand files, docs, and updates. The repository in their hands.

If you have two offers that attract different buyers, consider two clusters rather than one blob. A founder buying a marketing site and a founder buying a product interface overlap, and the studio can say so. They still ask different second questions. Let the second questions live in the right set. Cross-link when the buyer might be both people. A page with two honest links is not an orphan. A page with twenty anxious links is a directory.

## What a small studio should do first

Publish the hub only when two or three spokes are good enough to link. An empty map is a content calendar disguised as a page. It tells a visitor you intend to be useful later. They are here now.

Then keep the rule that prevents the mill: no page ships unless it answers a question the others do not, in language a founder would respect, with at least one link that earns its place. That rule is slower than a production line. It is also the only way the author page, the feed, and the search result all describe the same studio.

When you want to see whether your offer and your questions are one cluster or three, book [an intro call](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min). Bring the list of decisions a buyer has to make. The call should show you which pages are real and which are only keywords.

A cluster only works if you can finish the pieces. [How often a studio should publish](/blog/how-often-a-studio-should-publish) is the next piece, because a plan for fifty pages means nothing if the pace that keeps them good is two or three a week.
